question: Which statement best describes Landmark elements?
options: <div> and <span> carry no meaning — they're generic containers for styling/scripting hooks. Reach for a semantic element when one fits the content's role, and fall back to div/span only when none does. 'Div soup' (everything a div) is valid but loses all the structure semantics provide.

An <article> is a self-contained, independently distributable piece (a blog post, a comment, a product card) — it would still make sense pulled out on its own. A <section> is a thematic grouping of related content, usually with a heading. If the chunk could stand alone, use article; if it's just a labeled region, use section.

Headings h1–h6 create the page's outline. Use exactly one h1 for the page's main title and don't skip levels (h2 then h4) — assistive tech and SEO rely on a logical heading hierarchy to convey structure. Style with CSS instead of picking a heading level for its size.

Elements like header, nav, main, aside, and footer define page 'landmarks' that screen readers expose for quick navigation. There should be exactly one <main> per page, and landmarks let users jump straight to the content, nav, or footer without tabbing through everything.

question: Which statement best describes section vs article?
options: Semantic elements have built-in roles (a <nav> is a navigation landmark, a <button> is focusable and keyboard-operable) so assistive technology can announce and navigate them correctly with zero extra ARIA. Using the right element is the first rule of ARIA: prefer native semantics over adding role attributes to divs.
